title: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves

questions.prompt: Name the electromagnetic region between infrared and ultraviolet, and state whether its waves are transverse or longitudinal.
Which statement best describes a plane-polarised wave?

options.A: Its direction of travel is restricted to one line.
options.B: Its oscillations are restricted to one direction perpendicular to travel.
options.C: Its frequency is reduced by a filter.
options.D: Its oscillations become parallel to travel.

questions.prompt: A wave travels east and is plane polarised with vertical oscillations. Which direction describes its energy transfer?
Why can a longitudinal wave not be plane polarised in the same sense as light?

options.C: Its oscillations are parallel to its direction of travel.
options.D: Its speed is always too low.

questions.prompt: A plane-polarised radio wave travels horizontally towards a detector. Its oscillations are vertical.

figure.purpose: Assess separation of propagation, oscillation and transmission-axis directions.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white line diagram. Show a horizontal beam arrow entering a circular filter frame. Leave the transmission axis blank for the learner to add. Do not include oscillation arrows or alignment labels.
figure.alt_text: A horizontal radio beam enters a filter whose transmission axis has not been drawn.

parts.prompt: State the direction of energy transfer and the direction of oscillation.
Draw the transmission axis of a filter aligned with the wave, and explain your choice.

questions.prompt: A student observes that rotating a filter changes the signal received from an electromagnetic transmitter.

parts.prompt: Explain what the filter is restricting when the transmitted wave is plane polarised.
Explain why this observation is evidence that the wave is transverse. Do not use an intensity formula.

questions.prompt: A laboratory compares a light beam with a sound wave in air. Both travel from left to right.

figure.purpose: Assess an original transverse-longitudinal comparison and polarisation conclusion.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white two-row diagram. Top row: a straight light-beam travel arrow with an empty box for oscillation arrows. Bottom row: evenly spaced air particles with a travel arrow and an empty box for particle-motion arrows. Include no answer arrows.
figure.alt_text: Blank comparison rows show a light beam and a sound wave travelling from left to right.

parts.prompt: Add arrows to show one possible oscillation direction for the light and the particle-motion direction for the sound.
Use the accepted transverse-wave definition to classify the light wave.
Compare what happens when an ideal polarising filter is rotated about each wave's direction of travel.
